questions.q: What problem does Kappa architecture solve, specifically, from Lesson 6's Lambda discussion?
options: It avoids maintaining two separate implementations of the same logic by using one streaming codepath for both live and historical processing
It requires more codepaths than Lambda, not fewer
It replaces KQL entirely with a different query language
It eliminates the need for any streaming infrastructure at all
questions.explain: Kappa refuses to have two codepaths in the first place, unlike Lambda's separate speed and batch layers.

questions.q: How does Kappa architecture handle historical reprocessing?
options: Kappa architecture cannot handle historical reprocessing at all
By replaying old events back through the same streaming pipeline that already exists, rather than standing up a separate batch implementation
By manually re-entering historical data through a different UI
By running a completely separate PySpark job with entirely different logic
questions.explain: This mirrors Fabric Lesson 27's point about both ingestion paths landing in the same table, queried identically either way.

questions.q: What does Kappa architecture actually require in order to work at all?
options: A pre-existing batch layer to fall back on
The event source needs to be durably replayable — either through enough retention, or raw events durably stored somewhere replayable
Kappa architecture has no real prerequisites
A minimum of two separate Fabric Capacities
questions.explain: Without a replayable source, there's nothing to replay, and Kappa simply isn't an option.

questions.q: When is Lambda architecture still the right choice over Kappa?
options: When the speed layer's approximate answer and the batch layer's exact answer genuinely need different logic or engines
Only when the data volume is extremely small
Only when there is no streaming infrastructure available at all
Lambda is never actually the right choice once Kappa is available
questions.explain: Not every problem reduces cleanly to "one logic, replayed" — some genuinely need two different computations.

questions.q: Why is Kappa usually the preferred choice when it's actually available?
options: Kappa architecture doesn't actually involve any streaming components
Kappa is always cheaper to run than Lambda regardless of scale
Kappa requires no retention or replayability considerations at all
It avoids Lambda's codepath-drift risk entirely, since there's only ever one implementation of the logic to maintain
questions.explain: One codepath means no risk of the speed and batch layers silently computing the same thing slightly differently.
